items.title: US study tests psilocybin to fight cancer side effects
items.summary: Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: Beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.

items.title: A black hole as light as 40 tons can exist inside a star if dark matter helps
items.summary: In 1974, Stephen Hawking made a prediction that transformed our understanding of black holes. Black holes, he showed, are not truly black: They slowly lose energy through a quantum process now known as Hawking radiation. The lighter the black hole, the faster it evaporates.

items.title: Tree species diversity protects forests from climate extremes, study finds
items.summary: New research has found that tree species diversity can play a crucial role in protecting forests from the growing threat of extreme climate events. items.title: Scientists discover how narwhals grow nature's only straight tusk
items.summary: Narwhals have nature's only straight tusk, a single tooth up to three meters (10 feet) long, so strange they were sold as magical unicorn horns during the Middle Ages.

items.title: Some disagreement makes groups more trustworthy, mathematical framework finds
items.summary: When humans are making decisions, they are known not to rely solely on their own considerations and the evidence available to them. Past behavioral science and psychology studies have shown that people are often also influenced by the choices and opinions of others.

items.title: Lakes aren't just storing water—they're changing the carbon cycle
items.summary: Lakes may look like picturesque stopping points along a river or stream, but they can have a big influence on what happens to carbon as it moves through a landscape. items.summary: Has El Niño reached the West Coast? You might think it has. After all, the ocean off Southern and Central California is unusually warm. items.title: Late Roman decrees uncover military system behind amphitheater animal spectacles
items.summary: A study on Roman law by the Carlos III University of Madrid analyzes the regulations and complex imperial logistics governing the capture, transport and safety of animals used in spectacles in the Roman Empire—which were far more popular than gladiatorial combat.

items.title: New method predicts where massive earthquakes will strike
items.summary: UC Riverside scientists have developed a way to identify where Earth's biggest earthquakes are most likely to occur, offering a powerful new tool for improving disaster preparation in some of the most dangerous seismic regions.

items.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
items.summary: Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago battles fires that have burned large swaths of Borneo and Sumatra for weeks.

items.title: Indonesia rescues second orangutan mother and baby from wildfire
items.summary: An orangutan mother and her baby, threatened by wildfires encroaching on their habitat in Indonesia, were rescued earlier this week, authorities said in a statement Saturday.

items.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins 'tricky' arrival
items.summary: After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the monthslong, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the sun-scorched planet.

items.title: Levitated magnet opens new frontier in search for ultraheavy dark matter

items.title: AI could undermine managers' judgment unless used carefully, study warns
items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has become a routine part of working life, but overreliance on the technology may erode managers' ability to build moral insights, contextual understanding and know-how to get a job done, according to a new study from the University of Bath.

items.title: Study reveals pupils most at risk of school suspension and what may help them
items.summary: School suspensions are associated with a complex combination of socioeconomic disadvantage, special educational needs, peer relationships and students' experiences of school, according to new research from The University of Manchester.

items.summary: The catastrophic flooding in July 2021 claimed the lives of more than 200 people in Germany and Belgium. items.title: Scientists overturn a theory about this shark’s strange head
items.summary: Scientists have overturned a leading explanation for why male and female bonnethead sharks have differently shaped heads. Instead of males developing a pointed snout at maturity, both sexes actually begin with more pointed heads that become rounder with age, particularly in females.

items.summary: Researchers at Lund University have developed a new type of light-emitting diode based on thin, branched nanowires that could offer significantly higher efficiency and lower production costs than current technology. items.summary: Harvard researchers have transformed ordinary knitting into a platform for creating fabrics that can snap between different shapes and perform useful functions. items.summary: Why do some ants help nestmates in distress while others don't? items.title: Magic-angle graphene provides evidence for unconventional superconductivity
items.summary: Researchers have completely suppressed superconductivity in magic-angle graphene by screening interactions between electrons, helping resolve a long-running debate about the origin of the phenomenon.

items.summary: In a paper published in the journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, researchers at Kyushu University report on what happens when wharf roaches, a common shoreline scavenger, eat expanded polystyrene (EPS). items.title: Do games make children more attentive or more distractible?
items.summary: A study of preschool children found that brief digital or traditional gameplay improved performance on tasks requiring quick responses but reduced performance on tasks demanding greater concentration and self-control.

items.title: Periodical cicadas may be doomed to extinction
items.summary: Every 13 or 17 years, swarms of cicadas emerge from the ground, their black bodies, orange-tinged wings and ruby-red eyes enveloping trees and forests. It is a biological marvel unique in the insect world, and when it happens, it is impossible not to notice.
